text: Fervor is intense, passionate enthusiasm — the energy of fans camped out overnight for tickets. The Court's conservative justices haven't just accepted originalism; they've embraced it with new fervor, which is exactly why lawyers are now racing to find historical evidence for every case.

To abridge is to cut back or restrict — often rights and freedoms (it can also mean shortening a book). The word is in the First Amendment itself: Congress shall make no law “abridging the freedom of speech.” Originalism's defenders say tying judges to the original meaning is the only way to stop them from abridging rights the Constitution guarantees.

Archaic means belonging to a much earlier time and no longer in use — the “thee” and “wherefore” tier of old. To win a 2026 voting case, lawyers dug up archaic legal tracts and 19th-century dictionary definitions of the word “election” — writings so out-of-date almost nobody reads them anymore.

A court's docket is its official list of cases waiting to be decided — its to-do list. The Supreme Court's is “chockablock with tough cases” right now because June is when the justices race to finish their biggest decisions before summer break.

Chockablock means crammed completely full, with no room left — originally a sailor's word for when a pulley's ropes were pulled tight as they could go. A docket chockablock with cases is stuffed to the brim.
A tankard is a big, heavy drinking mug with a handle, often made of pewter or silver — the kind you picture in a colonial tavern. John Adams reportedly drank one full of hard cider with breakfast.

“Hard” here means alcoholic: hard cider is apple cider that has fermented into an alcoholic drink. In the founders' era it was an everyday beverage — which is Gorsuch's whole point about John Adams's breakfast.

When a question “turns on” something, that thing is the hinge the answer swings on — it all depends on it. Whether states can count late-arriving mail ballots may turn on a forgotten Civil War voting practice. Nothing to do with a light switch.

A postmark is the stamp the post office prints on mail showing the date it was sent. A ballot “postmarked on time” was mailed before the deadline — even if it arrived after Election Day, which is exactly what the fight is about.
Judges on the Supreme Court are called justices — there are nine of them, and their leader is the Chief Justice. Same job as a judge, fancier title.
Ascendance is a rise to power or dominance — to ascend is to climb. The “ascendance of originalism” means the theory has climbed from one philosophy among many to the one that now drives the Court.

The legal philosophy driving the whole article: the Constitution's words should mean what they meant to the people who wrote and approved them — not evolve with the times. The rival view, a “living Constitution,” says meaning should adapt as society changes. Under originalism, history becomes courtroom evidence, so lawyers end up working like historians.

Fashionable here means popular and in style among thinkers — ideas have fashions just like clothes do. Originalism has been fashionable in conservative legal circles for decades; what's new is a Court majority acting on it.
A supermajority is a lot more than half — a dominant bloc. Six of the nine current justices are conservatives, so on ideologically split cases that wing doesn't just win, it controls the outcome.

A classic trivia board game where you win by knowing obscure facts. The article's joke: historical tidbits that used to be good only for game night are now ammunition that can decide Supreme Court cases.

The part of the Constitution (ratified 1791) protecting the right to keep and bear arms — the legal foundation of every gun-rights fight in America. A 2022 ruling said modern gun laws survive only if they match early American traditions, which is why these cases now run on history.

The forefront is the leading edge — the very front of the action. Second Amendment cases are at the forefront of the history-hunting trend because the 2022 ruling made history the official test for gun laws.

To amass is to pile up a large quantity of something over time — a dragon amasses treasure. Lawyers are amassing “historical ammunition”: stockpiling old laws and documents to fire at the other side in court.

Literally, ammunition is bullets — but figuratively it's anything you can use to attack or defend in an argument. “Historical ammunition” means facts from the past used as weapons in court, a sly image in an article about gun cases.

To decree is to order something officially and with full authority, like a king issuing a decree. Saying the Court “decreed” its history test emphasizes that the rule came down from on high and everyone below must follow it.

A law is constitutional if it's allowed under the Constitution, America's highest law — and unconstitutional laws get struck down by courts. Under the 2022 test, a gun regulation is constitutional only if it matches early American historical traditions.
Pending means not yet decided — hanging in the air, waiting. A dispute “pending before the justices” has been argued or filed but the Court hasn't ruled yet.

Oral arguments are the live courtroom sessions where lawyers for each side make their case out loud and get grilled with rapid-fire questions by the justices. That's the setting for Gorsuch's hard-cider speech — justices often use their questions to signal what they're thinking.

A parallel is a situation so similar to another that you can line them up side by side, like parallel lines. Drug addiction wasn't a recognized concept in the 1800s, so the justices hunted for a founding-era parallel: how the law treated heavy drinkers.

The leaders who created the United States — writing the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution — like Adams, Madison and Jefferson. “The founding” means that whole era, roughly the 1770s–1790s, which originalism treats as the source of the Constitution's true meaning.

Habitual means done constantly, as a habit; a drunkard is a person who is regularly drunk (the same mocking “-ard” as in “coward”). Early states passed laws stripping rights from “habitual drunkards” — the closest old parallel anyone can find to today's ban on drug users owning guns.

Intoxicants are substances that make you drunk or high — alcohol and drugs both count, which is the point: Gorsuch's suggestion is that if using intoxicants cost you your gun rights, the hard-drinking authors of the Second Amendment would have been disarmed themselves.

An advocate is someone who publicly argues for a cause — to advocate is to speak up in support. The advocates of originalism defend its strange-looking history hunts as the only honest way to read the Constitution.

A legislature is a body of elected lawmakers — Congress nationally, or a state's assembly. The article pairs them with judges as the two forces originalists want to stop from whittling down constitutional rights.

To ratify is to formally approve something so it takes legal effect — constitutional amendments only count once the states ratify them. The “ratifiers” are the people who did that approving, and under originalism, what *they* understood the words to mean in 1868 is what matters.

A police “sweep” of cellphone data is a broad grab that scoops up information about lots of people at once, the way a broom sweeps up everything on the floor. The same image returns later: whether the 14th Amendment was meant to “sweep as broadly” — cover as many people — as it does today.

A warrant is a judge's written permission letting police search or seize something — the Constitution generally requires one before the government can go through your stuff. Here the fight is over warrants ordering Google to hand over people's location data.

Akin means similar in nature — literally “of the same kin,” like family. The lawyers debated whether modern data warrants are akin to the searches British customs officers used to harass colonists — because if they're alike, the founders' objections apply.

Customs officers are the officials who inspect goods coming into a country and collect taxes on them. Before the Revolution, British customs officers could ransack colonists' homes and ships with near-unlimited search papers — a grievance that helped inspire the Constitution's limits on searches.

To wage is to carry on a war or campaign — you wage battles, not play them. Saying the ballot fight “is being waged on a battlefield from 160 years ago” keeps the joke going: a modern election case fought entirely on Civil War ground.

To squabble is to argue noisily over something small — siblings squabbling over the remote. Using it for top Republican and Democratic lawyers fighting about Civil War voting details is the writer being a little mischievous.

The Civil War practice at the center of the ballot case: Union soldiers voted from their army camps in the field, and the ballots were carried back home and counted after the election. If that was legitimate then, maybe late-arriving mail ballots are legitimate now — that's the argument.

In the Civil War, the Union was the North — the states loyal to the U.S. government — fighting the Confederacy, the Southern states that broke away. Union soldiers were the ones voting from the field.

Apt means exactly fitting or appropriate — an apt comparison is one that genuinely matches. The whole ballot case boils down to whether Civil War field voting is an apt precedent for 2026 mail voting, or a comparison that only looks right.

A precedent is a past decision or practice used as the model for deciding a current question — if something was accepted before, that's an argument for accepting it now. Courts lean on precedents to keep the law consistent, which is why each side hunts for historical examples that resemble its own position.

A brief is a written document lawyers file laying out their side's arguments and evidence — despite the name, they're often anything but brief. The briefs in the ballot case are “riddled with citations” to a forgotten 1915 book.
Riddled with means shot through with — full of holes or full of something, the way a target is riddled with bullet holes. Briefs riddled with citations are stuffed with references on every page.

A citation is a formal pointer to a source — the courtroom version of the footnotes in your research paper. Lawyers cite books, cases and documents to prove their claims; here they're citing an obscure 1915 book and 19th-century dictionaries.
Obscure means little-known, hidden in the shadows — from the Latin for “dark.” An obscure 1915 book by a Boston lawyer sat unread for a century until this case suddenly made it courtroom gold.
A tract here is a short written work arguing a point — an old-fashioned pamphlet or essay — not a tract of land. “Archaic legal tracts” are dusty old legal writings the lawyers exhumed for evidence.
To hinge on something is to depend entirely on it — a door swings on its hinge, and the biggest case of the term may swing entirely on history.
A bid here is an attempt — a push to achieve something, as in “a bid for the championship.” President Trump's “bid to end birthright citizenship” is his attempt to end it; no auction involved.

The rule that nearly anyone born on U.S. soil is automatically an American citizen — citizenship as a birthright. It was written into the 14th Amendment in 1868, mainly to guarantee citizenship to formerly enslaved people; the case asks whether it really covers children of undocumented immigrants.
Undocumented immigrants are people living in a country without the official legal papers — the “documents” — that authorize them to be there.

To enshrine something is to fix it in a protected, almost sacred place — a shrine — so it can't easily be touched. Rights get “enshrined” in constitutions: birthright citizenship was enshrined in the 14th Amendment in 1868, locking it into the country's highest law.

One of the Constitution's most important amendments, ratified in 1868 after the Civil War: it guarantees citizenship to people born in the U.S. and equal protection under the law. The birthright-citizenship case turns entirely on what its authors meant that year.

“The administration” means the president's government — the White House and its officials, not office paperwork. Here it's the Trump administration arguing that birthright citizenship was never meant to sweep so broadly.

To dust something off is to pull it out of long storage and put it back to use — literally wiping off the dust. The administration dusted off old newspaper articles and speeches to defend its position; the article hints many historians find those sources unrepresentative.

An artifact is an object surviving from the past — usually a museum word, which makes it pointed here: one of the administration's key “artifacts” is an unsigned, undated, unpublished letter someone found in President Andrew Johnson's papers. Not exactly a smoking gun.

A treatise is a long, formal, scholarly book examining a subject in depth. The 1881 treatise cited here comes with baggage: it was written by a former Confederate officer who wanted to deny citizenship to Chinese immigrants.

The Confederacy was the group of Southern states that broke away from the U.S. in 1861 to preserve slavery, starting the Civil War; a Confederate officer fought on that side. Citing one as your authority on the 14th Amendment — written specifically to protect freed slaves — is exactly as awkward as it sounds.

Irony is when reality lands the opposite of what you'd expect. The irony here: Roberts, the one conservative justice who won't call himself an originalist, may love history more than any of them — he majored in it and dreamed of teaching it.

A buff is an enthusiast — someone who geeks out on a subject for fun (the word supposedly comes from New York fans of firefighting who wore buff-colored coats). A history buff devours historical books and trivia, which Chief Justice Roberts very much is.
An undergraduate is a college student working toward a first (bachelor's) degree — “undergrad” for short. As an undergraduate at Harvard, Roberts majored in history.

To punctuate a speech with something is to sprinkle it throughout, the way punctuation marks dot a sentence. Roberts routinely punctuates his speeches with historical anecdotes — little stories dropped in at regular intervals.
An anecdote is a short, entertaining true story — the kind that starts “that reminds me of the time…” Roberts collects historical ones and works them into his public speaking.

The solicitor general is the federal government's top courtroom lawyer — the official whose job is to argue the government's cases before the Supreme Court. “Solicitor” is an old word for lawyer, like “counsel.”

To pepper someone with things is to fire them off rapidly, like shaking pepper — or buckshot — all over. The solicitor general peppered the court with historical citations, one after another after another.

Something falls flat when it completely fails to impress — a joke nobody laughs at. All those historical citations fell flat with the chief justice, who called them “very quirky”: polite Supreme Court language for “unconvincing.”
